reels.title: A new pipeline in an hour

beats.say: Why does starting a new data pipeline take six weeks in some companies?
Teams copy an old repository, file tickets for a schema, a connection and alerts, and wait. A template asks a few questions and creates a working repository in one step.
It asks only what it cannot guess: the product name, the domain, the owning team and the schedule. Everything else has a safe default.
The result runs on day one, with tests, alerts and an owner already in place.

check.q: What should a template ask the team?
opts: Only what it cannot infer, like name and owner
Every setting the pipeline could possibly use
Nothing at all; teams fill files in later
check.why: Few questions and safe defaults make the template fast and consistent.

work: Time how long your last new pipeline took to reach production.
List the questions a template would need to ask.

reels.title: What a template creates

beats.say: What is inside a good data product template?
A standard layout, a pre-filled contract, a transformation project with one working example, and tests for the contract, data quality and code.
Then CI with policy checks, the orchestrator job as code with retries and alerts, monitors to the owner, catalog registration and a README.
Defaults matter most, because most teams keep them: retries, idempotent writes, a dead-letter table and schema checks.

show.title: Defaults teams keep
show.text:
retries: 3
write: overwrite_partition
dead_letter: true
schema_check: contract

check.q: Why do template defaults matter so much?
opts: Most teams keep them as they are
They are required by law in most places
They make the template much smaller
check.why: Defaults decide how most pipelines behave in production.

work: Write the defaults your template would set.
Check one of your pipelines against them.

reels.title: Templates drift

beats.say: You fixed a bug in the template last month. Did the fix reach any of the teams that already used it?
A template is copied once. A year later, eighty repositories came from six versions, and last month's security fix reached none of them.
Version the template, record the version in each repository, and let a bot open upgrade pull requests with tests running.
Better still, copy less: shared CI and deployment workflows update everyone in one place.

check.q: What reaches every repository fastest with a fix?
opts: A shared workflow referenced by version
A copied file in each repository
An email asking teams to edit by hand
check.why: Shared workflows update in one place; copied files must be upgraded one by one.

work: Find which template versions your repositories are on.
Move one copied CI step into a shared workflow.

reels.title: Choosing what to put in a template

beats.say: Should the template copy every file a team needs into the new repository, or should some parts live elsewhere?
Copy what each team will change: the contract, the model, the README. Reference what must change for everyone at once: CI, deployment, policy checks.
Every copied file is a file you will upgrade eighty times. Every referenced one is upgraded once.
Say this split out loud in a design interview: it shows you have run templates for years, not weeks.

check.q: Which part should a template reference rather than copy?
opts: The CI steps every team shares
The product's own contract file
The team's example data model
check.why: Shared steps change for everyone, so they belong in a versioned shared workflow.

work: Mark each file in your template as copy or reference.
Count the copied files you would have to upgrade.

reels.title: Golden paths in one minute

beats.say: Thirty teams, thirty ways to build a pipeline. Is that a problem?
A golden path is the opinionated, supported way to do a common job, end to end. It bundles the decisions most teams should not have to make.
Three properties make it golden: it is the easiest way, it is supported by the platform team, and it is optional.
Teams may leave the path, but then they own what they build. Paths win by being better, not by being mandatory.

check.q: Which property is part of a golden path?
opts: Teams may leave it and own what they build
Every team must use it with no exceptions
Only the platform team is allowed to use it
check.why: Golden paths are optional; they win on speed and support.

work: Name one job your teams do thirty different ways.
Write what the golden way would be.

reels.title: Which journeys to pave

beats.say: A platform team cannot pave every road at once. So which journeys should it pave first, and how does it decide?
List what teams do, how often, and how long it takes today. Pave the journeys that are both frequent and painful first.
Before building, shadow two teams doing the journey the hard way. Every wait and copy-paste goes on the backlog.
One or two journeys done really well beat ten journeys done badly and left to rot.

check.q: Which journey should usually be paved first?
opts: One done 20 times a quarter taking six weeks
One done twice a year taking two days
One that changes completely every month
check.why: Frequent and painful journeys repay the investment fastest.

work: List your teams' five most common journeys.
Write how often each happens and how long it takes.

reels.title: Guardrails, not gates

beats.say: Should a review board approve every new pipeline?
A gate is a person who must approve. A guardrail is an automatic check that stops a mistake and says how to fix it, on every change.

show.title: Wait for a person, or *check in CI*

beats.say: Good guardrails: the contract exists and matches the data, personal data is masked, there is an owner, tests pass, costs stay in quota.
Every guardrail needs an escape hatch: a waiver with a reason, an owner and an expiry date.

opts: It has an owner and an expiry date
It is approved once and kept forever
It is stored in a separate wiki page
check.why: An expiring waiver turns an exception into a dated decision.

work: Turn one manual review into a CI check.
Add expiry dates to every existing exception.

reels.title: The developer portal

beats.say: Golden paths are useless if nobody can find them. Where do teams go to start something new?
A developer portal, often Backstage, brings together a catalog of everything, templates behind short forms, docs next to the code, and scorecards.
Scorecards show each component against the standards: owner, contract, tests passing, a supported template version, service levels met.
Do not let the portal and the data catalog compete. One place to start beats two half-complete ones.

check.q: What does a scorecard in a developer portal show?
opts: Each component against the standards
The salary bands of each team
Only the cost of the platform team
check.why: Scorecards make standards visible per component.

work: List the five checks your scorecard would show.
Decide whether portal or catalog is the front door.

reels.title: Measuring a golden path

beats.say: The golden path exists and the template works. But is anyone choosing it, and is it saving them time?
Track adoption for new projects, time to first production run on and off the path, lead time and change failure rate, support tickets, and satisfaction.
If adoption is low, ask why before you mandate anything. Usually the path misses a real need, or it is slower than the old way.
Low adoption is a signal about the path, not about the teams.

check.q: Only 15% of new pipelines use the template. What first?
opts: Ask teams why they skipped it and fix that
Make the template mandatory right away
Build several more templates at once
check.why: Fix the reasons teams leave before mandating anything.

work: Compute adoption of your templates last quarter.
Interview one team that skipped the template.

reels.title: How golden paths fail

beats.say: Most golden path programmes fail in the same few ways. Learn all of them before you build your first template.
A golden cage that cannot bend. Too many paths, none maintained. Stale templates nobody upgrades.
A path built without asking users. Gates disguised as paths, still ending in a ticket. Defaults nobody understands or can debug.
Each has a fix: escape hatches, fewer paths, upgrade bots, shadowing users, automatic guardrails, and docs.

check.q: The template still ends with a ticket to the platform team. What is this?
opts: A gate disguised as a golden path
A normal and healthy golden path
A golden cage with an escape hatch
check.why: Self-service means no waiting on a person for the common case.

work: Check your paths against the six failures.
Remove one ticket from your most used path.

reels.title: Mandate the path or not?

beats.say: A director wants every team on the golden path by next quarter.
Agree with the goal, not the mandate. A mandate turns the path into a cage, and teams with real exceptions route around it.
Mandate the guardrails instead: owner, contract, masking and tests apply to everyone, on or off the path. Keep the path itself optional.
Then make the path the default in the portal, and retire support for the old ways with a date.

check.q: What should be mandatory for every team?
opts: The guardrails such as owner and masking
The template and the tools inside it
One orchestrator chosen by the director
check.why: Rules apply to all; the path stays optional and earns adoption.

work: Write which rules you would make mandatory.
Set a retirement date for one old way of working.

reels.title: Owning a platform as a product

beats.say: Who owns the golden paths, and who pays?
The platform team owns the templates, the scaffolder, the shared workflows and the upgrade process, with a roadmap and support. Teams own what they create.
Do not build a path for a journey that happens twice a year, or for tools changing every month. Write a guide first, pave later.
Retire a path when its journey disappears, or wrap a managed service that does it better.

check.q: When should you write a guide instead of building a template?
opts: When the tools change every month
When thirty teams repeat the journey
When the journey takes six weeks today
check.why: A template for fast-moving tools is out of date in weeks; pave later.

work: Name the owner of each template you have.
Find one path you should retire.
